title: The One Machine Every Chip Needs (And Why Only One Company Can Build It)
description:
The chip in your phone has billions of switches, each smaller than a virus. So who builds the machine that draws them? One company in a small Dutch town: ASML. This video follows the full story: how lithography works, why engineers kept chasing shorter and shorter light, how a TSMC engineer's water trick pulled ASML ahead, and how extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light is made by blasting tin droplets with a laser fifty thousand times a second. See the mirrors from Zeiss, the lasers from Trumpf, the light source from Cymer, the leaky-shed start in 1984, and the thirteen years it took from prototype to production. Then learn why nobody can copy it, how Dutch export controls keep EUV out of China, and what High-NA EUV means for the next generation of chips.

Research behind this video: Jay Lathrop and James Nall, first photolithography work at the U.S. Army Diamond Ordnance Fuze Laboratories (1957-1959); Gordon Moore, Cramming more components onto integrated circuits, Electronics (1965); Hiroo Kinoshita et al., NTT, multilayer-mirror EUV reduction imaging (1986-1989); Burn J. Lin, Immersion lithography and its impact on semiconductor manufacturing (2004); EUV LLC consortium (1997); Chris Miller, Chip War (2022); ASML and Zeiss technical publications.
